utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-00-39-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Stewart, is the Defence ready to continue its cross-examination of the witness Deronjic? Yes, then, the witness may be brought into the courtroom. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, at the conclusion of yesterday's session, Your Honours asked about a specific minute and whether it was already in evidence, and I can inform Your Honours that it is -- the minute that is referred to by Mr. Deronjic is found in Prosecution Exhibit 39. I have prepared extra copies of Prosecution Exhibit 39 which can be distributed to you, and you will find reference to that particular meeting of the municipal board that was held in Kravica on the 22nd of January 1992 on page 13 of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's part of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now I feel a bit less ashamed of myself not to know exactly what is in the book as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But the reference is on page 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Deronjic, I apologise for not -- doing something else when you entered the courtroom. Please be seated. It might sound familiar already to you, but nevertheless I would remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you made at the beginning of your testimony, and you certainly will remind my words spoken at that very moment. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, good afternoon. You told the Chamber yesterday that in Bratunac, you had adapted Variant B because you weren't able strictly to follow the instructions set out.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stewart. Yes, that's correct, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you also said that you decided to maintain contacts with Muslim representatives.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Mr. Zekic aware of the maintenance of those contacts?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did -- he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did he raise any objection?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we completely disagreed about it. I can just say that he did not apply Variant A and B in Srebrenica at all, and I think that the reason for that was that there wasn't an adequate number of Serbs in the joint organs of authority, and he felt that this should not be done. I was able to discuss this with him, and he simply did not interfere in what we were doing and how we were doing things in Bratunac. He's a man whom I know well, and he's not very systematic in his work, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now moving to a different topic, then, you -- in your evidence earlier in this hearing, you said that in the course of the summer in which you were talking about, 1991, you said that there was some activities which you implemented and that was the arming of the people. And you said that a large number of the population at the time on one side and the other were armed. Those were your words. First of all, when you talk about one side and the other, can we be clear who it is you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I said that a large number of the population was armed, including one side and the other, I was thinking of the Serbs in Bratunac and the Muslims in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in 1991, in the summer, are you able to give any indication of the relative scale of arms bearing by the two sides, Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could tell you what I know. Of course, I don't know precisely the number of Serbs who were armed, and it's hard to say to what extent the Muslims were armed. However, some events from that period, or rather clashes practically open conflicts, even though a slightly milder term could be unrest in Bratunac caused by various political developments stirred up the ethnic tensions or national tensions in the municipalities so that at one point in unrest developed into open conflict, including two killings. From late August until the late fall and the beginning of the winter of 1991, 1992, the town was practically under barricades, and it was very difficult to control the situation in the field. It was difficult for the police to do so. I will mention that at one point, because of the killing of two Muslims in Kravica, Bratunac was visited by top representatives of the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities. Mr. Koljevic came to Bratunac representing the Serb side. Mr. Ostojic on behalf of the SDS, and Mr. Ejup Ganic. I think he was at the time he was the vice-president or something. But anyway, he was one of the key figures in the SDA. And Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we just pause a second, Mr. Deronjic. Can we put a date on that, the particular incident in Kravica? Or can you put a date on it, is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's September. I don't know the exact date. I have it written down somewhere. If you remind me, perhaps I could give you the exact date tomorrow. But it was in September that the killing of two Muslims occurred in Kravica. The circumstances are well known, if you are interested, or the Trial Chamber, in finding out more details I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we can just try and put a date on it then. If I suggested to you that it was, in fact, Saturday, the 31st of August 1991, would you be prepared to accept that that was the date?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could accept that. I said September, but now you've helped me, so we're talking about late August. That's the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then in early September, that delegation arrived that you described. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was -- what was the purpose of their visit?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of their visit was the unrest in Bratunac, those two killings. They came, and they were forced to land in Bratunac in a helicopter because Bratunac was blocked on all sides. All the villages -- in all the villages, people erected barricades. The tensions were especially high between Glogova from where the two people who were killed in Kravica were, and the village of Kravica. There were barricades all over the place, including in the town itself. There were barricades in a number of streets. In that period, I went to all those places with the representatives from Sarajevo who came. I went to Kravica, to Glogova, I was in Bratunac town also. We addressed the Muslim citizens. And we could see that both sides had weapons, and they were publicly carrying those weapons. We saw numerous people with weapons on barricades of each of the sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll come back to barricades if I may in a moment. But so far as this delegation was concerned, this high-level delegation, did they inquire or investigate into the events which had occurred as you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They asked questions, and they asked me to tell them exactly what happened. I talked with all of them individually, and also separately with the Serb side and the Muslim side. So I did provide the answers to what the cause of all of those conflicts was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did that delegation pronounce any conclusions as to what had happened in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than visiting Glogova, Mr. Hebib and I visited Glogova, and we addressed a gathering in Glogova which was attended by a large number of people. And then I also visited Kravica with the Serb representatives, and also addressed the people there. No other measures were undertaken over those few days. Several days later, the Bratunac security station staff was replaced, including the chief and the commander. I think that people were brought from outside, from Tuzla, I think, to take charge of that security station. These were the measures that the delegation carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did they in any way look into the question of the scale of arms which were held by Muslims and Serbs in that locality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have to say that at one point we discussed this at the municipality, and it was noted that there were too many weapons in Bratunac, that everybody there personally saw those weapons. Neither side was interested in the details of how this arming came about. It was just a fact that was noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were you able at that time yourself to have any -- well, I'll rephrase it. What degree of knowledge did you personally have about the scale of arms which was held in the first place by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was difficult to control. Of course, we knew that the Muslim side was arming itself. We monitored this, and I think that they also knew that we were arming ourselves. Sometimes at joint meetings, we would accuse one another. They would accuse us, and we would accuse them. So this was an open secret in Bratunac, that we were all armed. To what extent, I am not able to say, but I personally knew about it, and I had and I still have to this day with my lawyer the minutes of an SDA meeting in Bratunac in early 1992 in which they are distributing weapons and communications equipment in local communes and different settlements, and they are saying how many pieces of weapons were delivered to each village and how much was due to arrive. I still have those minutes today, and I think they're in the possession of my lawyer. I'm saying this, but it's true that each side was arming itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, in relation to a different locality, we've heard in the course of this case a description of arms being held by Muslims as being hunting rifles and not very much more than that. Would that description of largely hunting rifles being held by the Muslim community, would that be an accurate description of the situation in the Bratunac locality in the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally, as well as the gentlemen who came to Bratunac, could see all kinds of weapons, including automatic weapons in Glogova. They could see that at the barricades. At the meeting I attended in Glogova, also you could see the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were such weapons of that type in the hands of both the Muslim community and the Serb community?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Glogova is populated by Muslims, so the weapons were held by the Muslims. In Bratunac, you could see automatic weapons at the barricades. And the barricades were either those of the Serbs or the Muslims, and each side had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And these barricades, the word is a fairly simple one, but could you give some -- perhaps a little bit more description of the nature of these barricades and the effect they had on the life of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It did seem incredible, but this is what happened. After the killings in Kravica, throughout the town and the municipality, people were erecting barricades and posting sentries. When I say barricades, I'm thinking of barriers placed across roads and thoroughfares. For example, in Kravica they knocked down a tree to block the road. And they left a small space so that cars could pass by. In Glogova as well. I toured all of these places, so this is how I know the details. They brought out heavy forestry machinery, large tractors out on the streets. The machinery that handles large tree trunks. So you had to be very careful in traffic. It proceeded with caution so that everything was under control. In Bratunac, there were barricades in practically every street out of fear that open conflict could start. You could see in the streets that people had brought out objects. For example, they brought horse carts and left them on the streets, or old trucks, old cars so that they could have control over the traffic flow. And I saw numerous people with weapons at those barricades. At one point, I myself was in a very unpleasant situation because I was not able to go through a barricade. It seemed to me that I would get killed because I lost my way. I came into this street trying to avoid other barricades, so I couldn't get out of it. What I'm trying to say is the situation remained dramatic, and it remained so until the end of that year. The barricades were up for quite a long time. For example, the police would enter one street to do their work, and the guards posted on the street, whether they were Muslim or Serb depending on the situation, would even stop the police, and sometimes they would even talk to them. The police would speak to the people with the weapons in a good-natured way. And sometimes, actually most times, they would allow the police to pass. But sometimes it happened that they would turn them back. After these events, we would sit down together with the Muslim side often and discuss that with them so that already in early January or late December, the situation had calmed down a little bit and some of the barricades were dismantled and taken off the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: These barricades were to -- on the edges of particular sections or neighbourhoods of the town, were they? In one case a Muslim area and in another case a predominantly Serb area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There were some streets or some neighbourhoods which were populated by one population group or the other. And I can mention which streets and which barricades these were and who the area was populated by. I can say, for example, that guards would -- from a Muslim checkpoint would go to talk to guards at the Serb checkpoint. There were some absurd situations. People were communicating amongst themselves, but they kept -- they held on to their weapons for fear that somebody would do something to them. That's what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And these -- did these barricades, they may not have been totally unchanged, but barricades remained, did they, in Bratunac and in neighbouring villages right through until April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the fall, just before winter, I think this was sometime in December, we managed to dismantle these barricades, but people continued to keep sentry. I know that in Bratunac there were guard duties. There were no longer any barricades, but people would be on guard. For example, a man would stand guard at his own house. During the day, he would go and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say: "We managed to dismantle the barriers at the end of 1991," does "we" mean the local police, or who else does "we" mean?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were joint efforts. I have to say that at the time when we're talking about the SDA leadership, their key figures, the president of the municipality, Mr. Nijaz Dubicic, I had a series of contacts, not only I, but other people, too, from the organs of authority on the Serb side. A series of meetings also attended by the members of the police. And I can say that they did not support any of this, neither did we. We were asking for these barricades to be removed and for life to return to normal so that the police could do their work, including the investigation into these killings, which was a pretext for these conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you said in your evidence earlier that all these events, and you were talking at that time of really the second half of 1991, took place against the background of the open war raging in the Republic of Croatia, which was followed closely in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that the effect of the war in Croatia on the events in Bratunac was direct because some people, both Serbs and Muslims, went to those fronts as volunteers. And I know that perhaps ten young men, whom I knew, perhaps there were more - I don't know - they went to Croatia to the front from the Serb corps, but there were also many young Muslims who went as volunteers to the fronts in Croatia and fought on the Croat side. When they returned from the front, they brought the atmosphere of the front back with them, so we had disputes also about this matter. To us Serbs, it was inconceivable that the Muslims, in a war which wasn't their own, participated on the Croat side. But they had their own reasons for this. In return, they accused us of our young men going to war in a different state. But this was not a mass occurrence. However, for various reasons, people did go to these theatres of war. When I say various reasons, I'm thinking of looting, robbery, different motives. The people who went there had different motives for doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, in your evidence on -- well, it was yesterday, of course, you referred to the affair involving Mr. Spegelj, in the arming of Croats in Croatia. First question on that is -- before I ask you any more about it, did that affair have any impact on the Bratunac locality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indirectly, yes, but it is a very stretched link. If you're thinking of the arming, yes, there was a lot of pressure for the Serbs to get armed. But I don't think that there was any direct link, any direct effect on the actual war events in the area. However, the dissatisfaction --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I interrupted, Mr. Deronjic. You said: "However, the dissatisfaction."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, what I was trying to say was that this caused great dissatisfaction amongst the Serbs. The newly elected authorities in the Republic of Croatia, because of this arming which we considered to be a direct threat to the Serbs in Croatia. This is how this whole thing was interpreted over the media, and this was the interpretation that we were receiving from the top levels of authority. And this is why we received an image of the situation which may have been erroneous. But in the final analysis, this caused major dissatisfaction amongst the Serbs in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I was really in a sense trying to avoid going too much into something which you confirmed didn't have a direct impact on Bratunac. But in the light of the last few answers, I really had better ask you, then, to tell the Tribunal as briefly as you can what was the affair involving Mr. Spegelj and the arming of Croats in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably know actually. I don't know how much you know. But this affair was a matter of public knowledge, and it was published and broadcast in the media that Spegelj participated in the arming of Croats in Croatia at the time when the common state of Yugoslavia still existed. This arming, these weapons came from the neighbouring countries through various channels, and the State Security Service followed this, and they even managed to shoot some of the activities. And I had opportunity to see the footage of this affair involving this arming.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I've got to ask you about something else now, then, Mr. Deronjic. You said -- when you were talking about the pressure, you talked about -- well, I don't want to misquote. You say -- you talked about fear, Serbs arming themselves because they were fearful of the possibility that during the breakup of Yugoslavia certain things which had happened in the past could happen again. And you said that people were under a lot of pressure to rearm. And then you said: "Then again, there was the pressure on the people because they did not fully trust the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA." Who was it who didn't trust the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to answer only the question concerning the JNA? It seems to me that you have asked several questions. If you want me to talk about the JNA only, I can certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't intend to ask several questions, so I'll refine it then. The question was you referred to there being pressure on the people to arm because they did not fully trust the Yugoslav People's Army. And I'm asking you who it was who did not fully trust the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a large number of people within the Serbian Democratic Party who did not trust the Yugoslav People's Army. When I say, "A large number of people," I'm not only referring to the membership, to the members. I cannot speak about that. I am referring to the officials of the SDS. Both at the local and the regional level in which I participated. And also on the basis of my knowledge from the top republican level of the party, I knew that there was a difference in opinion as to the future role of the JNA. You're probably aware of the fact that a lot of SDS members were anti-communists, and they considered the army to be part of the previous, former regime, and that it was a big question mark whether they would be willing to side with the Serbs in the implementation of the programme, in the implementation of the nationalist objectives. Such opinions were frequently expressed, and I often was able to hear criticism from the members of the main board, criticism which was levelled against the JNA and the fact that they were not able to adopt themselves to the present moment, the actual political situation and the events as they were unfolding on the ground. So apart from the failure to adapt ideologically, I have to say, so that it should be perfectly clear, that the JNA was still multiethnic. Their leadership, but also the rank and file were multiethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I want to ask you about decisions that you took that you referred to in Bratunac in early May of 1992, and two particular decisions you referred to. One was a decision banning the activities of all paramilitary formations in the territory of Bratunac, and the other was a decision allowing the police legally to disarm illegal groups which appeared in the locality. Now, you remember giving evidence about those two decisions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Mr. Zekic aware of those decisions being taken?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that he knew about the first decision. As for the second one, the one of the 13th of May, Mr. Zekic was already dead. He died on the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... Yes. Yes, I beg your pardon, the second decision came a few days later, so of course that would follow. So in relation to the first decision, did you ever hear any protest or objection or dissent from Mr. Zekic in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Zekic on the 4th or the 5th of May. Unfortunately, this was the last time I saw him. So I really cannot say what his view was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My question was whether, in fact, he indicated any dissent or opposition to that first decision.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting in the Fontana Hotel, I did not mention this decision at all. We discussed the overall role of the volunteers and the plans that they seemed to be receiving from someone. That was the essence of the discussion. He didn't make any comments, nor did I raise any particular issue with respect to that. No, he did not give any comment to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters are kindly asking Mr. Stewart to come closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You referred earlier in your evidence to a disarming plan, and you said that after -- Captain Reljic took control, and that was in April -- middle of April 1992, according to your evidence, he was issuing commands. And then in late April, so we're talking about 1992, certain activities occurred out in Muslim villages, and in particular collection of weapons in Muslim villages and warehousing of those weapons at a depot of the police station in Bratunac. Were you involved in any way in that collection of weapons and warehousing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Not only that, I took part in one such operation of disarming as a soldier. I did not have any particular function at that time, and I had been mobilised as a soldier. And I participated in the action of the disarming of the village of Podcaus, as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And -- well, let's take that village, Podcaus, to start with. Did your involvement in that enable you to form any view of what the scale of arming and arms bearing had been in that village in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the village is Podcaus, and it is actually almost a suburb of Bratunac in the direction of Srebrenica. I was not able to gain any insight into that. I mean, I was with the troops, with the soldiers, in a forest far from the village. It was members of the military and the police who actually entered the village and carried out the disarming itself. However, later, when I became a member of the municipal Crisis Staff, I was able to check the quantity of the weapons that had been seized during that operation. I think that most of those weapons were hunting rifles and various kinds of trophy weapons which were first stored at the police station in Bratunac, but then moved to the Zvornik police station. So I think the exact number can be established. According to the information that I had, I think that we were talking about 300, or perhaps a little more, rifles that had been surrendered by the Muslims during this operation of disarming in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And those 300 came from a -- can you say, came from a population of how many approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 22.000 residents who were Muslims in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And are you able to give any further information about the scale of arms bearing in the vicinity of Bratunac at that time, in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have any direct knowledge of that. In April 1992, I did not have opportunity to count them. But it was a large quantity of weapons. I have indirect knowledge coming from the testimony of some Muslims, even in my case, who mentioned the fact that they had buried a certain amount of weapons. Again, no numbers were mentioned. But there are indications that they had secret caches of weapons. I'm not trying to strike any kind of balance here. But the fact remains that they had weapons. If you want me to be precise, I think that the Serbs had more weapons than Muslims in Bratunac; however, as a result of their numbers, Muslims in terms of the number -- the size of the population, the Muslims outnumbered Serbs. But they had weapons as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you, please, Mr. Deronjic - and I indicated this exhibit earlier to the Tribunal - to have a look, please, at P47. Do you have that, Mr. Deronjic? It's -- you have been asked about this before, a decision on strategic objectives of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you were asked -- Mr. Harmon asked you, as I'm asking you now, to focus on strategic objective number 3 on that list. And Mr. Harmon asked you if you'd like to comment on the statement made by Mr. Kertes in April of 1991 in Belgrade in this particular strategic objective. And you said: "Yes, Mr. Harmon, I think these things are connected," that's Mr. Kertes's statement, "perhaps not in this form, refers to the strategic decision of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And I'm just wondering what -- if you could say what you meant by "perhaps not in this form"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, here, it says: "To establish a corridor in the Drina River valley," that is, to eliminate the border, which is clearly stated in item 3 of this decision. Kertes uttered a sentence which was rather outspoken, but it was not a precise rendering of what and how it should be done. He didn't use these same words. He just said 50 kilometres from the Drina River, the area will be completely Serb. So although the words were not the same, the idea is exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, turning to something else, I just want to ask you about, do you recall that meeting you've given evidence about when you went to Pale in May 1992, and you made a report which included a reference to what had happened in Glogova. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you already described quite a lot about that meeting. You received some sort of applause at that meeting, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What sort of applause was it? Was it polite applause for an efficient report? Was it in the nature of some enthusiastic, unusual congratulation? What -- how was it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be perfectly frank, my impression was that this was a form of congratulation on the job that I had done well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What had you reported to the -- because you described to the Tribunal you had a private discussion later about it. But how much had you actually reported to the meeting about what had happened in Bratunac and in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the population of the village of Glogova had been forcibly moved out. I'm not sure I used the exact expression, but it was perfectly clear that they had not left on their own, of their own free will; that the village had by and large been burned down; that there had been a lot of destruction in Glogova as well; that the operation of the forcible removal of the Muslim population would continue the next day in Bratunac and the neighbouring villages. That was the essence of my statement. I cannot remember all the details. I also indicated that I did not have information regarding the killings in Glogova, and I did not inform them of that because I truly didn't know anything about that on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you described later on, Mr. Djeric was angry about that particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was very angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you say, what were the essential points that gave rise to his anger?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything. The fact that the population had been forcibly removed, the fact that the village had been burned down, almost all of it. He was surprised at hearing this, and I think his response concerned all of this and provoked his anger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I want to ask you about something different, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness please could have up -- if we could have P52.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've seen this before, of course. This is a bank document. I just want to ask you -- it was put to you by Mr. Harmon. Do you know -- well, it's more than one page, but do you know any more about these documents than can be read by looking at them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I know was that Mr. Dukic, according to the stories that went around, was financing the SDS. I don't know whether anything else can mean anything. But I said that this document confirmed the widely spread opinion that he was one of the persons who financed the SDS. I don't know anything else about this document. I saw it only recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In other words, anybody else reading this document can get as much from it as you can, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say anybody else. Those who are familiar with the stories and the rumours, yes, perhaps. But what we see here is only the mention of payments, but we do not find anything about the purpose, the objective of these payments. At least, I cannot see anything that would indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let me put it another way: Of course, when I say "anybody," anybody who knows who Mr. Karadzic is, who knows who Mr. Krajisnik is and who knows that Deutsche Bank is a bank. But given those matters, what I'm putting to you, Mr. Deronjic, is that you don't personally know anything about any of the particular items or particular individual matters referred to in this document, do you, apart from what you actually see on the writing on the document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing. I don't know anything about these payments, items, but what I can see here. But I made a link with the widely spread opinion that Dukic was one of the financiers from the early periods of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just a different point altogether, then and we'd be finished with P52 for the moment. You described in your earlier evidence how you were asked for some help in relation to getting away from Bratunac. You were asked for some help by Mr. Dubicic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, give help to Mr. Dubicic, which was of practical value to him in getting away from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was that the provision of a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The vehicle belonged to the Bratunac public security station. He just asked whether this would cause problems if he were to take the vehicle, if they took the vehicle and left, and I said there should be no problems, that they could take the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't suggesting you gave him your car, Mr. Deronjic. But you -- so you gave your approval and authority to such a vehicle being made available to enable Mr. Dubicic to get away from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can say that, although it's a strange formulation that I approved it, since the chief of police was there. He's the one who disposes of the facilities of the station. I know that some people wanted to stay and some wanted to leave Bratunac. But I didn't find anything strange about that. I said that if you have any problems, you can always cite me, if you have any problems in Kravica. And I know that they did mention my name in Kravica, and then they left for Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I've no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Is there any need to re-examine the witness, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: A few questions, Your Honour. If I may have the assistance of the usher to have the podium brought to me, I would appreciate it. We have one podium for the two sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have P48 shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I would like to show you some entries in the diary of Mr. Jankovic. I just invite your comments on this particular set of entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I have prepared for Your Honours the Jankovic diaries in hard copy, and I could direct Your Honours' attention to the portions that I'm referring to. The exhibit is P48.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I want you to look at these particular entries. I will invite your comment in a minute. And it deals with a question that Mr. Stewart put to you on -- it's on page 27 of the LiveNote transcript that I have, as to whether you had any contacts with Mr. Krajisnik from 1990 onwards. And you said in your answer that you had never had any opportunity to contact Mr. Krajisnik personally in that period. And I would like to refer you to the Jankovic diary. I'm referring you to the entry that starts for January the 12th. You will find that, Mr. Deronjic, if you could read -- if you could read the diary entries and -- you are signaling me that that may not be the right exhibit. Is that correct? If you could read the entries, Mr. Deronjic, let me continue my question. It will be on the B/C/S version of the diary on page 1 to the end of page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be found on page 2 of the English version. It will go through -- midway through page 4, the English version. To assist the Court, I have a copy. I can just let the witness use my B/C/S copy. It's difficult to locate in what is currently available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that the Defence would agree that we expect Mr. Harmon to give exactly the same copy as the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, if you could take a look at the entry in Mr. Jankovic's diary, the entry I'm referring to is the entry from January the 12th, 1991. And if you could read that entire entry. It ends at page 5 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, are you just asking me to read what it says on page 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you to read the entry that starts on -- entry for January the 12th, 1991. That should start on page 1. Do you see the entry for January the 12th? If you would read that complete diary entry.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Yes, I've read the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you could read the complete entry for that date. That should carry you over, Mr. Deronjic, to the end of page 5. The entry ends, Mr. Deronjic, just before the new entry dated January the 13th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just above the entry for January the 13th, it indicates that a group of persons were to leave for Sarajevo to negotiate with Karadzic. And your name is mentioned in item number 4. Do you see that reference?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, if you would turn to the entry that is dated January the 15th, 1991, in the English version it is found on page 5. In the version before you, Mr. Deronjic, it is found on page 9. And it's dated January the 15th, 1991, and there's a -- and I'll make it easy for you -- easier for you, Mr. Deronjic. I will just read it. It says: "Talks in Sarajevo. The meeting began at 1800. The meeting was attended by Karadzic, SDS president; Krajisnik, BiH president; Velibor Ostojic, Dukic (sick with ambition). Karadzic started the talks by a lesson regarding forming a party within a party and regarding not consulting him about that." I will not read any further, Mr. Deronjic. But as I read and understood the entry on January the 12th, a delegation went to see Mr. Karadzic on the 15th in respect of the SDS -- the creation of the SDS regional board in your region. You were selected to be one of the participants in that meeting, and that meeting occurred a number of days later in Sarajevo along with Mr. Krajisnik present. So does that, Mr. Deronjic, refresh your recollection? Do you recall attending such a meeting with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. I mentioned this meeting in a conversation with you during the interview I provided, but at the time I could not remember all the participants. It's true that I attended this meeting, and I remember Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic at this meeting. I mostly focussed on what President Karadzic was saying, and I think that I said that he was very angry because in his opinion we formed this region -- this regional board on our own initiative. Yes, this meeting did take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was interested in correcting the answer that you gave that you never had any opportunity to contact Krajisnik personally in the period of time that was referenced by Mr. Stewart, which was the period of time of 1990 onwards. So let me ask you, Mr. Deronjic, what was the role of Mr. Krajisnik in that meeting? What was his participation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember his participation. I don't remember him saying anything, but I do remember that he was present. We were criticised by Karadzic, and Dukic presented the main problem there because he wanted to have his own informal power in Eastern Bosnia, and this is where the disagreement came from. I don't really remember it all that well. The role of President Krajisnik there was one of the leading officials of the SDS. That's what we thought at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, I'm referring to the entry on January the 15th, 1991. It says, and I quote: "When we presented everything that we had done, everyone but Dukic was left breathless. Karadzic and Krajisnik congratulated." Can you expand on what that means, "Karadzic and Krajisnik congratulated"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Petar Jankovic is a very strange person. I don't know whether we amazed them with our abilities or our political work. I really don't think that. But probably we discussed some economic activities, and they felt pleased about that. Jankovic was always talking about establishing a bank. He always wanted to set up a bank. Jankovic, before the outbreak of the conflict, left Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was in a dispute with the SDS leadership at the time. I know that he was ambitious in order to become a leading figure in the SDS. He had burning ambition. But I would not really take this that seriously, that they were breathless. I don't know what it was so great that we did. We were criticised for some conduct about a certain meeting in Dubica, but I really recall very little of this. And I don't remember them congratulating us. That could be the precise answer. I don't remember anybody congratulating us on anything during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see it is 3.30. Is this the usual time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we usually have one and a half hour until the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me just to add one sentence, because I can see from -- I'm sorry. I'm sorry, I'm reading the minutes. He says that Dukic lost control. It's true that there was a conflict between Petar Jankovic and Dukic. And I'm remembering the meeting now a little bit. The main discussion was between him and Dukic. Dukic practically reported us as being undisciplined in the field, and this is when there was a dispute between Dukic and this Petar Jankovic. I apologise for adding this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, would you please verify with the witness that in the original that in my translation it says: "Ajkic is losing control and having hysterics."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, let me direct you to the entry on January the 15th, 1991. That should be on page 9 of the B/C/S version before you, and there is a sentence that I read to you: "Karadzic and Krajisnik congratulated." In the English translation in the next sentence, there is a name. It starts the first sentence. It says the name "...is losing control and having hysterics." Can you tell us what the name is in the B/C/S version before you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Mr. Rajko Dukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me take you down to the next -- the two sentences later, the sentence that starts with: "Our delegation reached a conclusion that it was all..." Can you tell me the name that follows?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. I've concluded with this document, Mr. Deronjic. Let me take you to another part of your testimony. One point during your cross-examination, Mr. Stewart identified for you the positions that were -- that you were aware of that Mr. Krajisnik held during the period of time between 1991 and 1993. And you identified the following positions. You said he was the Speaker of the BH Assembly, he was the Speaker of the Republika Srpska Assembly, he had a membership in the Personnel Commission. And then you added that he was also a member of the SDS Main Board. And that is the sum total of your recollection when you gave that testimony. Let me ask you, Mr. Deronjic, are you familiar with a body known as the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know of a body called the Supreme Command. This body existed in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did that body exist in the period of 1991 to 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the dates from when until when it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you aware if Mr. Krajisnik was a member of that body?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I know that at one point Mr. Krajisnik was a member of that body. And thank you for reminding me, but I really wasn't able to remember that. I didn't really have the opportunity to think about that. But that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you aware of a body known as the National Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if we're thinking of the same body. I think that that is the council -- I'm not sure whether these are two different bodies. Perhaps there were two different bodies. I always thought that there was -- that was just the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What knowledge do you have as to Mr. Krajisnik's membership in the National Security Council? If you don't know, you don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a little bit difficult to see what the witness is going to say since he has already answered a question in relation to a body called the Supreme Command, and then expressly said that he thought this one was the same body. So to be asked about Mr. Krajisnik's membership of what Mr. Harmon is putting forward as another body when the witness is not accepting and not saying that there are two different bodies is really inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour, it's inappropriate. But it's certainly -- I will withdraw the question. This is not an area that is contested. This has been a -- this is an admitted fact that is before this Tribunal. So I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, are you aware of the existence of a body known as the expanded presidency?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that body, but I don't know any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me take you, then, to another area of your cross-examination. And you were asked by Mr. Stewart, and you affirmed to Mr. Stewart, that you had never heard Mr. Krajisnik express any racial hatred toward anyone. Do you remember that testimony? Racial or nationalistic hatred toward anyone, I think was the question. Is that correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever express any racial or nationalistic hatred toward anyone?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And nevertheless, according to your factual basis, you subscribed to a policy of creating Serb-ethnic territories within Bosnia and Herzegovina, and later to the use of force to remove non-Serbs from Serb-designated territories --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, is Mr. Harmon cross-examining his witness now, or is he re-examining his witness? Because, normally speaking, we would suppose that cross-examining your own witness has to be the subject of a special application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm cross-examining your witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cross-examining a witness, usually as far as I understand, but I'm not raised in the common-law tradition, that if you treat your own witness as someone that should be cross-examined on the answers he has given on cross-examination by the other party that you -- whether you need leave for that, or that you at least announce that. But announcement is made, and let me just confer with the other Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may examine the witness as you did, Mr. Harmon. I have to add to that, that the Chamber has noted that this is a subject, at least a subject matter that has been dealt with in cross-examination by the Defence. So this is not a -- this is not an opening for all subjects. But on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I simply -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. Of course we accept that ruling. So far as the subject being dealt with in cross-examination is concerned, the subject of statements by Mr. Krajisnik was certainly raised in cross-examination. Of course, that's precisely the point. The subject of statements made by this witness, such statements is not in the least bit touched on in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think it's a matter of reliability and credibility that is involved because if you have to judge upon -- if you have to give information on ever something -- well, let's say if you would consider that to be bad being said about another person, then your own position might be of influence for the situation. So therefore, Mr. Harmon is allowed to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you understand -- let me repeat my last question, Mr. Deronjic. You, nevertheless, subscribed to a policy of creating Serb-ethnic territories within Bosnia and Herzegovina, and later to the use of force to remove non-Serbs from Serbian-designated territories. That's correct, isn't it, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, I want to go to another part of your testimony. You referred to preparing maps for the Bratunac municipality with different colours. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the different colours identified different ethnic groups within your municipality. Can you identify for the Judges what colours were used to designate which ethnic groups in the maps that you prepared.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we used blue to mark Serb territories and green to mark Muslim territories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I think this is repetitious. I even remember that the witness said that there was no colour for Croats because there were hardly any Croats. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine, that was only one question. I didn't remember it. But I will pursue another line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you had a series of answers to one of Mr. Stewart's questions in which you discussed the Serbs in their arguments emphasising both historical arguments and landownership arguments. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the next exhibit, if I could have the next exhibit, please. It is an exhibit that has a list --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit Number P62.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: P62 could be distributed, then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm waiting for those copies to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, before you is P62. Do you recognise that particular document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is represented by P62?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is information about the arable lands in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the ownership of that land. We distinguish between three categories of ownership: Serb ownership, Muslim ownership, and social ownership which existed as a form of ownership in the earlier period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you assist in the preparation of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember the details. I said we made it. Probably I helped in some way. I probably did help in the compilation of this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. And where were lists like this sent?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We passed all the information to the technical service in Sarajevo, the technical section of the SDS. Everything was sent to the party presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I notice it is a quarter to 4.00 now, Your Honour. I have only a couple more questions after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps the Bench might have some questions as well. We'll adjourn until five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be brought into the courtroom. Please be seated, Mr. Deronjic. Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I only have one additional matter to cover with you. And it deals with Variant A and Variant B. As you recall, that document is -- bears the -- in the upper left-hand corner, the Main Board, and it's dated the 19th of December 1991. If I could have the next exhibit shown to the witness and given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit Number P63.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There should be a sufficient number of hard copies for the Judges, if those could be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, P63, for your information, is a set of minutes of the session of the Serb People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Assembly. It is an Assembly session that was held on the 11th of December 1991, eight days before the issuance of Variant A and Variant B. And I would like to direct your attention to subpart 2 of that -- of those minutes, the part that reads: "A draft recommended (decision) on setting up municipal assemblies of the Serb People in BiH." Do you find that section in the minutes before you? It should be very early on in the document. Mr. Deronjic, I think it is on the page that bears the ERN number in the lower right-hand corner of 00183447. If you could read subpart 2 in its entirety; it's not long.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention, Mr. Deronjic, to the top of the page bearing the ERN number 00183448, to the paragraph that reads -- it should read as follows: "The Assembly --" and this, Your Honour, is found on page 3 of the English translation, three paragraphs from the bottom, reading from that particular paragraph: "The Assembly's President, Momcilo Krajisnik, once again underlined the need to set up Serb municipalities where the Serbs are a minority without any obligation to do the same in all municipalities." Mr. Deronjic, I invite your observations on that particular paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without any specific guideline, I don't think I can add anything in particular. I know that this concerns Variant A and B, and one can see that this was discussed. I have already indicated that these variants, according to this document, envisaged Variant B, that is, the formation of parallel Serb organs and municipalities as well. This was actually an order to establish Serb municipalities, and I implemented this order in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, do you see any connection between this -- the minutes of the Bosnian Serb Assembly session and Mr. Krajisnik's -- the paragraph that I identified for you, and Variant A and Variant B, which was issued eight days later?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. There is a connection. It can be seen clearly from this. It means that this material was discussed at this session, and that, among others, the Assembly's president, Mr. Krajisnik, also discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Deronjic. I've concluded my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Judge Canivell has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a few things. First of all, you said that in a meeting at which you thought of resigning, you were promised that an aspect that you saw in the instructions you had received wouldn't be applied immediately. And that made you reconsider your further decision. Where did they come, these promises, from the highest personalities in the SDS, or from where that these promises came?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I have to apologise to you, but I think that the interpretation that I received was not completely clear. I don't think the -- your question has been interpreted in its entirety. So I should like the interpreter to repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Does the interpreter need me to repeat what I asked? Well, I will repeat it. You said that you were promised that some of the measures that were suggested to introduce in -- you remember the A and B alternatives and first and second stage of this document, you received some promise that some of these measures wouldn't be implemented immediately. And that's why you decided to reconsider your -- the resignation you had already tendered in your post in the staff in Bratunac. I would like to know who made you these promises.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for your question, Your Excellency. I now fully understand what you meant. I received these promises from the municipal board of the SDS in Bratunac, from an official of this municipal board. So I'm talking about the officials at the local level, that they would allow me to implement this variant -- these Variants A and B in the way that I suggested, which implied, which included talks with Muslims regarding this particular issue and an agreement to be reached with them concerning the partition of certain institutions. I insisted only that the police station should be divided into the Muslim and the Serb police station, which agreement was reached and was implemented at the level of the Joint Assembly in Bratunac. Formally speaking, two police stations were set up. However, they continued to work together in the same building and undertook a number of measures that had been agreed upon jointly with the leaders of these two police stations. So this is one of the promises that I received. This is how I wanted to proceed. This is how I thought this should be implemented. And it was at that point that I retracted my resignation and continued to implement this policy in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I have another question. You have mentioned at a certain point that rank and file members of the JNA were multiethnic. But at what moment you are-- you were referring, for one aspect? And besides, what proportion of ethnicities would be serving in those JNA forces?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try to answer your question as best as I could, Your Excellency, although I am not the right person to provide such analyses. In 1991, Muslims refused to be recruited into the JNA. In the summer of 1991, they refused the JNA recruitment. Before that, it was the Muslim population that was mostly being recruited and mobilised into the JNA because they were the predominant population. However, I think that after 1991, a very small number of Muslims remained in the JNA because they had refused to serve in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: And finally -- thank you. Finally, you explained, but I didn't understand completely well, that at a certain moment, you said Serbs had more weapons than Muslims. But I don't know if you were speaking in general or you were referring to in relation with the number of Serbs and the number of Muslims, or what you really meant at this moment? Do you remember the point? You had mentioned it while you were being cross-examined by Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Excellency, I fully remember my testimony. I merely wanted to show that both sides were arming themselves. My opinion is that as far as the percentage is concerned and the ratio between the weapons and the populations, Serbs did have more weapons. However, because of the fact that Muslims were more numerous, one could say they had a large quantity of weapons as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, I should like to ask you a few questions in order to ensure that I understood you properly and that I followed your testimony properly. My first question is as follows: I'm interested in what was mentioned at the very beginning of your testimony concerning a certain number of inconsistencies in some of your statements. Could you please very briefly inform me of the reason -- of the possible reason of such inconsistencies? Is it because you were not able to remember everything, or was it something else? I should like to hear from you what you think is the reason of these inconsistencies in your statements, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Excellency, when we talk about the previous statements given to the Prosecutor, let me just remind you of the fact that it was in 1997 that I started giving statements to the Office of the Prosecutor. They concerned mostly the events in Srebrenica. In a testimony here before this Tribunal, I already indicated that I had not provided the whole truth in some of those statements. I did tell the truth; however, not the whole truth, concerning one of my conversations and meetings with Mr. Karadzic because I believed that this could endanger me and my family. So this was the reason why I had failed to mention this detail concerning this conversation between me and Mr. Karadzic. As for the remainder of the statements that I have given, I tried as best as I could to be consistent. However, it is very difficult for me to have full control over everything that I said, over all of the descriptions of the events that I provided, especially when it comes to the use of specific terms and specific wordings. It is possible for these minor inconsistencies to have taken place because of the interpretation. I understand that this is a rather difficult and complex process because even for me it is very difficult to find the right word sometimes for what I want to say. So I think that this could also be one of the reasons for these inconsistencies. It was never my intention to improvise in any way, and I believe I can support everything I said with adequate proof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much. So if I understand you correctly, you have just reassured us, and you have confirmed that you have been telling the truth, that everything you have told us is true and correct. Let me move on to my second question concerning your intention to offer your resignation at one point. You said, if I understand your testimony correctly, that you had intended to resign because you did not approve of the methods that had been envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is more or less the essence of my motives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have been provided with a transcript -- rather, a report of the 22nd of July 1992 [as interpreted]. I will read it out to you because there may have been a mistake in translation or interpretation. And I quote: [In English] "New option of communist Yugoslavia." [Interpretation] This seems to me to be a bit too removed from the reasons that you offered for your resignation. The text does not reflect this motive that you have given to us. I should like to hear your comment, your answer to this.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me first draw your attention to the fact that the meeting lasted the entire day, and it was frequently interrupted with many discussions and debates. This is just a brief report of the meeting. The minutes were kept by a secretary of the party, not very educated man, and he recorded what he thought had to be recorded. As for the reasons of my resignation, I also believe that I mentioned Variants A and B as well. I have to say that we, in Bratunac, acted on my proposal and implemented this Variant A and B in a completely modified manner. Otherwise I don't know why we would have acted the way we did. But among other things, I also criticised the policy of Milosevic, Karadzic, and Babic, I believe, was mentioned in this context as well. Because I had had previous disagreements with these policies; in particular, the policy of Mr. Milosevic. On that occasion, I expressed the opinion that Mr. Milosevic was not working in the interest of the Serbian people, and I also expressed my opinion that he had ideological reasons to act the way he did, that he wanted to have a state which would again be a communist state and so on and so forth. So it was a rather long session, a rather long meeting which involved a number of discussions and debates. And the person who took the minutes recorded only a small portion thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your explanation. Speaking of Variant A and B, let me draw your attention to a question which was asked of you by the Prosecutor. You answered as follows, and I quote your words: [In English] "One was to implement measures to create Republika Srpska because Variant B implies the establishment of parallel institutions at the municipal level. And when I say 'parallel,' I mean purely Serbian as opposed to the institutions that were in place at the time, whereas in Variant B it implied the association and linkage of Serbian municipalities into one entity." [Interpretation] At the beginning, you spoke only of the Variant B, and then all of a sudden you say: "On the other hand, in Variant A," which means that you either made a mistake or you wanted to say Variant A at the beginning, and then Variant B as opposed to what you had already indicated. Or maybe you wanted to say that it was only Variant B which required two measures to be taken at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this is an unintentional contradiction. I would actually like to modify this and say that this was implied in both variants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me one additional sentence concerning the meeting that we discussed a moment ago, because I just remembered something. So with your permission, I should like to add just one more sentence regarding measures A and B and the meeting at which I tendered my resignation. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you continue, I think you will be able to read a comment which will enable you to understand the situation better. The president of the Serbian Assembly in Bratunac and a member of the municipal SDS, Ljubisav Simic, says: "If necessary, we will refuse the orders of the presidency of the SDS, and we will not betray the people we have so far led in the direction that we deemed to be the right one." And because there are no other orders but the ones that we received, he was obviously referring to those orders. He even says at one point we're going to refuse to obey both Sarajevo and Belgrade, and we will continue with the policy that we think is adequate in light of the circumstances and the situation as it is in Bratunac. This is what I wanted to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. When he spoke of the instructions coming from Sarajevo, who exactly did he have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubisav Simic, the president of the Serbian municipality in Bratunac, and a member of the municipal board of the SDS in Bratunac, he wanted to say that we would refuse these orders if they were not in conformity with our needs and the circumstances of our situation. And he referred to Variant A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but who issued those orders?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received the orders from the presidency of the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me move to a different topic concerning the operation, or rather the events which took place in Glogova. If I understand you correctly, you decided at one point to open up a corridor between Bratunac and Kravica. You said: "We decided." Who did you have in mind? Who took this decision?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was referring to the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bratunac of which I was the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But were you prompted by someone else? Did you receive directives or orders from someone else, from elsewhere? Or was it you? Did you make that decision and were you in charge of the implementation of that decision?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for you to better understand my testimony, I made this decision on that night at the Crisis Staff without having received prior directives to that effect. I, likewise, never asked any guidelines for the implementation of this directive, save for the consultations that I had had with Goran Zekic who was a member of the board and who was a deputy in the Assembly. And also with this person who was a link with Serbia and its state organs, Mr. Predrag Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the night, at one point you just had an idea that night that you had to adopt this decision, and you carried out that decision the next morning?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in the factual basis, Your Honour, and in my interview -- that in late April, beginning of May, I had given this idea some thought and that I had discussed it with Captain Reljic, who was the military officer on the ground, and that we went on a reconnaissance visit to the village of Magasici on the 7th. So I had prepared this action with the military, but the actual decision to proceed with the operation was adopted at the meeting of the Crisis Staff of the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But generally speaking, a decision of such a significance, would it require consent or approval from higher level?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What higher level would that be? What higher level of authority?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at that point it would have been the republican leadership, the top leadership of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it your opinion or your conviction?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my conviction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When was this approval conveyed to you, or this order? It was either an order or an approval, if I understand your testimony correctly.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the approval from Mr. Zekic. He was the only representative of the Serbs in the republican organs at the high level. I asked him whether this was okay, and he said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me move to another subject. If I understand you correctly, you went to Pale at one point to give your report of the events that had taken place in Glogova. You told us that General Mladic was among those who were present at this meeting, and he wanted you to indicate on a map the exact location of the village of Glogova. Now, if I understood your testimony correctly, General Mladic was a military chief, and the fact that he requested you to point the location of a village on a map seems to me a bit confusing. I mean, it is difficult to understand that the military chief would not be perfectly familiar with his area of responsibility. Didn't you think it strange? Were you not surprised by his question?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Let me explain. General Mladic became chief of staff of the VRS on the 15th of May. This meeting took place either on the 10th or the 11th of May. Unfortunately, I cannot remember the exact date. And I thought, and this is what I already explained, that this was the first time that General Mladic was being briefed about the situation in Bosnia. And that was the reason why all presidents of the Crisis Staff or presidents of the municipal board had been invited to the meeting. The idea was for them to brief General Mladic about the situation on the ground. That was my understanding of the purpose of the meeting, and I think that at that moment he was not at all familiar with the situation in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only that he was not familiar with the situation in Bosnia, but you're now telling us that he at that point was not yet appointed to the post of the chief of staff of the military. So in what capacity was he present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I arrived late to this meeting, and nobody introduced General Mladic to me. I knew him from the media. I knew who he was.
