I think that he was there in the capacity of a person who in two or three days would take over command of the Army of Republika Srpska because on the 15th of May, he was named as the commander-in-chief of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I think you will agree with me that he was a career military officer.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also told us that Mr. Djeric had had a different reaction compared to the one that you received at Pale. Could you explain to me in two or three words who he was, what function he had, and what power he actually wielded.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric was the prime minister of Republika Srpska in its first composition. And according to my belief, he didn't have too much influence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't you think that he acted on the basis of the information that you had provided to him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're thinking of exactly. Perhaps the question wasn't interpreted correctly. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I haven't phrased it properly. You provided him with a piece of very important information, and he reacted in a way which demonstrated his dissatisfaction. Don't you think -- didn't you think at that point that he would react on that, that he would act upon it, that he would see other people, other individuals who might have a certain influence on the situation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that. Mr. Djeric wrote down what I said in his work diary. He made no comment other than being angry. He was asking angrily, "Who ordered you that? Why did you do that?" That's the way he was doing it. I said that the war in all the neighbouring municipalities was such that this was also spreading to Bratunac, so I also did something which I believed I should do. And he wrote that down. He didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you alone during that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, Your Excellency. At each of the meetings, I was accompanied by the driver who brought me to the meetings. He entered with me to the first and the second meeting. On our way back to Bratunac, and I said his name before, so on our way back to Bratunac we commented on this difference in the positions and in the reactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This brings me to my last topic which concerns the issue of volunteers. You testified about the volunteers who were present in Bratunac. I have a few questions in relation to that. To your knowledge, who was paying for them? Where were they accommodated? And who paid for their expenses?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Excellency, the first group did not live in Bratunac, to clarify that immediately. The second group who arrived lived in various places in Bratunac and in abandoned Muslims houses. I don't know about the financing. I don't think anybody financed them. They financed themselves. They were mostly criminals who really did a lot of looting in that period. So I assume that's how they financed themselves. I also think that there must have been some way that they were financed through Serbia, from where they came. But I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning inhumane treatment and the fate of the detainees, are you aware of any incident in which the responsible persons were tried for what they had done or simply questioned?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any case of anyone being questioned or put on trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I've got a few questions for you as well. First questions relate again to the meeting where your resignation has been the subject of discussion. First of all, for the record, I saw that in English the question put in French by Judge El Mahdi refers to a meeting of the 22nd of July, where I think it's the meeting of 22nd of January. But in the transcript, it appears as the 22nd of July. Do we agree, Mr. Deronjic, that when you answered the question of Mr. -- of Judge El Mahdi, that you're referring to the 22nd of January meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also, there was a short quotation of the minutes of that meeting which is not fully complete, so I'd like to have that on record as well because the minutes read, where it comes to the option of a communist Yugoslavia, the full sentence reads: "I will rather accept the sovereign Bosnia than some new option of communist Yugoslavia." That's the full sentence read. Now, you answered about the minutes that were made by the secretary of the municipal board, a not-well-educated man. Can you tell us what the name of this person was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gentleman's name is Milenko Katanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you told us that this was not an educated person, but did you see these minutes, and did you ever correct them or made a note that they were not complete?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer for the first question is that I saw the minutes and I signed them. I made no corrections, because I believed that it reflected the essence. I did not really pay attention to the details. We did not correct any minutes. We didn't have the possibility of writing everything down. It was impossible to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The minutes of this meeting themselves say that it was Mirna Nikolic who took the minutes. What's your comment to that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were two secretaries in the municipal board. Ms. Mirna Nikolic and Mr. Milenko Katanic. I thought that they were taken by Milenko Katanic, but Ms. Mirna Nikolic is a party secretary. I don't think that she even has a high-school education, but she is about there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: She is not a well-educated man either, is she?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't dare to say that she was not educated, but I think she is able to note down everything that is stated at a meeting like that. You must take into account that sometimes those meetings of ours were such that discussions overlapped, and this was all part of a regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing I'm making clear to you, Mr. Deronjic, that you explained the quality of the minutes taken by referring to a man, not well educated. And from your answer now, I understand that it's a woman, and you certainly did not have that person in mind when you answered one of my -- the previous questions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also told us that, this was only the essence, because it had been -- and let me try to read it literally. You said: "Your Honour, let me first draw your attention to the fact that the meeting lasted the entire day, and it was frequently interrupted with many discussions and debates." At what time did the meeting start, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember these details, Your Honour. My memory is not such that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Deronjic be provided with the minute book. Would you, Mr. Deronjic, please find for me the meeting of the 22nd of January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you find any indication as to the time when this meeting started?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It states here that the meeting began at 1700 hours, which means that it's in the afternoon. And I notice that I did not say how long it lasted correctly. It started in the afternoon, but then it probably went on late into the night. I think that's the only thing that I can add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'll come back to the issue discussed in this meeting, and that is that you indicated that if there would be -- that Mr. Karadzic, Dukic, and Koljevic should come to Bratunac where they will clearly state what the national programme is and what the bottom limit is. Otherwise, it reads: "I'd rather hand in my resignation than betray myself." Could you tell us, what was unclear to you and what needed further explanation by Mr. Karadzic or one of the other persons mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you. I must say that the meeting mostly dealt with the issue of relationships with Milosevic and the policy regarding that. That was the central issue at the meeting. I did not want to participate in something that was not quite clear to me. Did that mean that the policy in Bosnia was created by Milosevic or by us? And if -- and whether the measures that we were implementing were something that we approved at top-party levels, or was it something that we did not even review or adopt? For example, it was quite clear that the programme of the Serbian Democratic Party was abandoned, and I think in one sentence here I say: "There is no Yugoslavia any more; there are no longer six republics." And that was our programme. And what I wanted to say was what was our programme now, it wasn't clear, at least to me and to the people in Bratunac where all of this would lead, where this new policy that was being created would lead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, was there any doubt in your mind as to whether the Muslims had to leave their villages and the area they were living in?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point, I didn't have any idea that they were supposed to leave the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So when you said that you might resign, it was mainly about future policy in the, may I call it, inter-Serbian relationship, that is Republika Srpska, at least, and the -- well, let me say Belgrade and Pale. That was your concern when you considered to resign if you didn't get any further explanation. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the reasons why I wanted to submit my resignation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in your testimony you answered to a question of Mr. Stewart that on point 6 of stage 1 of the B plan, which is "set up secret storage places and depots in local communities or populated places with a majority Serbian population for the storage of foodstuffs, et cetera." I think you were asked whether this was implemented or not, and I think that you answered that question by saying that you'd rather wait and keep the money apart so that you could buy the foodstuff whenever that would be needed. Were, finally, these food storages created, or were they not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That was a recommendation which was not implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was never implemented?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of anything other than it was a recommendation for this to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you were never involved in implementing the creation of food storages?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then ask you to look at the same document you have in front of you. I have to find it on my computer. One second. The minutes, but now not on the 22nd of January but the next meeting. Could you indicate to us when the next meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can check here. But I really don't remember all of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, please find the next one after the 22nd of January.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 24th of February 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Deronjic. Could I please ask you to read the last line of paragraph 4, "Other business." As a matter of fact, I'll read it for you. Three lines before, it's about Mr. Deronjic suggesting a few things. And then the last line reads: "He added that as much food as possible should be stored in exclusively Serb areas." That sounds very much as food storage in which you just testified that you never implemented any food storage programme. Could you please comment on this part of the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said that this was a recommendation which we received in the materials, and I conveyed the recommendation. Your question is if I knew whether such food depots were created, and I said that I didn't know anything about it. And I said that they were not. When you asked me whether I took part in the creation of these food depots, I practically did not do anything in order to create such food depots. But I did say at the municipal board that people should take care that there are food reserves at all of the various territories, but I don't think that anything was actually undertaken in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it say any of the various territories, or exclusively on Serbian territory?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, it states: "Exclusively Serb territories."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In your answer, you said various territories. Is that -- is it wrong in the minutes, or is it -- or was your answer a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably in what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So do I understand your testimony well? That you say that you have drawn the attention that as much food as possible should be stored in exclusively Serb areas, and that this has got nothing to do with food storage that was recommended to you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm thinking that there is a major misunderstanding here. It's possible that you received a wrong interpretation. It absolutely has to do with what we were suggested or ordered to do. And I'm just saying, Your Excellency, that I did not concretise the proposal in the sense that we made food reserves, or I don't know anything about that. I don't know if food was really concentrated and taken somewhere. I don't know about it. I don't know how we could have put it all together and taken it to some territory. As far as these measures are concerned, I proposed that something like that should be done. If people had money, they should make their own reserves, if that was possible for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take you to a different matter. You have testified about de-arming villages. I then asked you the question whether also Serbs were de-armed in those villages. And your answer was, and I'm now summarising, that these were exclusively Muslim villages. I did put the question to you in relation to the village of Podcaus, which is at the southeastern outskirts of Bratunac. Was that an exclusively Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very difficult for me to give you a precise answer because I don't know what that region includes. I know that that region to a vast degree is Muslim. I don't know if it's completely Muslim. I don't know to this day. Perhaps there is the odd Serb house there or perhaps some of the outlying settlements are mixed. But for the most part, the majority part, it is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps have the map - I haven't got a number here - the map of Bratunac in front of the witness. Yes, could it perhaps be put on the ELMO, if possible. Perhaps you could turn a bit, Mr. Deronjic, to the machine to the right of you. Could you just indicate to us what you consider to be Podcaus. Perhaps with the pointer. Yes, your finger is good as well. We see it just south of the word "Bratunac."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To where? When you were talking about de-arming Podcaus, what area did you have in mind? A larger area?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, for example, go to the east and see where it would stop.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me just find the east, the eastern part. Yes, here it is. The area of Podcaus is connected with the area -- with the suburb of Bratunac, Djanici, which is a Muslim area. Then there is the high point, the high ground, Caus, the highest elevation in the Municipality of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please point that out so that we can see it, with a pointer or a pen.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it. I didn't see when you pointed where would be the eastern boundary of what you considered to be Podcaus. That would go until where, up until where?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, I think. There is a Roma settlement cause Rakovac, but there are also Serb houses there, as well as a few Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, my question: Were Serbs also de-armed in Podcaus?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the answer is now a bit different from what you said earlier when I asked: "Were Serbs disarmed in such villages?" You didn't say they were not. Your answer at that time was that you referred to villages that were exclusively Muslim. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the difference. I indicated yesterday that Serb villages had not been disarmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked whether Serbs in villages that were disarmed were also disarmed in those villages. But it's not of vital importance whether you see the difference. But do you agree with me that your answer now in respect at least of Podcaus is a different answer to what your answer was on my earlier question whether in disarming villages, Serbs were also disarmed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't precisely remember the answer that I gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not going to insist that you answer my last question. I'll turn to a totally different subject, your visit to Bajina Basta. Do you remember that you testified that you were invited by Mr. Zekic to go there. What was the reason to go there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zekic sent me a message through a person who visited me at home, Mr. Milorad Popovic, a member of the Bratunac SDS. He said that Mr. Zekic had left me a message, that he had gone to Bajina Basta, and that I should get there as well because there was a meeting to be held in the building of the Territorial Defence of Bajina Basta. I took a vehicle from the power distribution company in Bratunac and went to Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so the meeting was the reason why you went there. You saw that the same kind of troops or men that later came to Bratunac came over a bridge into Bajina Basta. Is that -- did I correctly understand that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These men went to Skelani on the Bosnian side. So they went from Bajina Basta, which is in Serbia, to Skelani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, came from Serbia, and they came over the bridge. I take it the bridge over the Drina River. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you were told at that time that you could expect them to come to Bratunac as well. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember using these words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll check it for you over the break. One of the problems is that I have only partial access to my LiveNote in this courtroom because part of the testimony was given in another courtroom. You said that the same type of men appeared in Bratunac, but you didn't know where they came from or you didn't know who they were? Do you remember that you were asked about who they were, who came to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer to that question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the question that I was asked when Muslims asked me whether I could give them my guarantee. I couldn't because I didn't know those people. I could only make assumptions as to who they were. No one told me at the meeting who it was who had sent them, nor did they identify themselves. I mean, at the meeting at the Fontana Hotel. Goran Zekic only briefly introduced these people to me, and he said that the topic of the discussion was Srebrenica, that they had issued an ultimatum to the Muslims in Bratunac to abandon power. I didn't know who those people were; I didn't know who had sent them. I knew only that they had arrived with Goran Zekic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when you were in that meeting a couple of days before when you saw these people for the first time, you didn't ask, "Who are they"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And Zekic told me that they were volunteers who were supposed to enter Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Anything further than volunteers, or...

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just what he told me. He made a joke that they had been brought by Jokic and made some comments to that effect. But they were about to leave for Skelani. I stayed in this office briefly, and Zekic and I continued talking for about a minute or two when we got to Skelani. I immediately went back to Bratunac, thinking that I would soon have an opportunity to meet with Zekic again and bring up the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did you have such an opportunity?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 5th of May that I first had opportunity to discuss the issue directly with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that before these people came to Bratunac or after?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After their arrival.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So even when they arrived in Bratunac, did you ask Mr. Zekic again who they were, apart from just being volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The meeting was a rather unusual one. No one told me that we had a meeting that day. I received the information to come to the meeting, but we discussed some issues very briefly, and then I immediately went back to the police station to discuss further with the Muslims. But they soon arrived and then immediately left for Srebrenica. And I never saw Zekic again because he went with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, my question was whether you further asked him. You gave a long answer but... Could I understand the answer to be no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... My question was whether you asked Mr. Zekic again who they were. And I do now understand that your answer was no. Now, about you expecting these people to come to Bratunac as well, could you -- you said you had no expectation or no one presented you any perspective in that direction. Or could you tell us a bit more about how surprised you were when these people came to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was totally surprised because no one had told me. Of course, I could assume that Bratunac would be visited by someone because such things were happening in my surroundings everywhere. But I -- and I simply couldn't conclude on the basis of anything that Bratunac would be bypassed and that such a group would not appear in Bratunac. However, I was surprised because no one had told me that someone would come to Bratunac on the 17th, the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that you say, "I was surprised although I expected it to happen"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. I thought that a thing like that could happen, but I didn't know who would that be, when they would arrive, and I also thought that if this should happen I should be informed by someone about their arrival, that I would be told in advance as to what their mission would be in the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got no problems in accepting that you thought that it could happen. My question was whether you expected it to happen and when you had any idea of whether that would be after you-- whether that would come soon or late or a month or a week or -- I mean, what actually was in your mind apart from that something could happen?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Excellency, your question commands a longer answer, due to the complexity of the situation in Bratunac and my attitude to the policy coming from Serbia, which is something that I could discuss here for days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I'm not asking what was the basis for what you thought to be possible or what you expected; I'm asking you, did you just consider it possible that they could come or did you expect them to come? And if you thought it would be possible or if you expected them to come, would that be soon or late or whatever did you have in mind at that moment when you returned from your meeting with Zekic when you for the first time saw those people? What was on your mind as to what Bratunac might experience in the future in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My thinking at that time was that for some mysterious reason Bratunac was being bypassed, starting from Bijeljina and moving further south, you have the events in Zvornik, and then nothing happens in Bratunac. And all of a sudden, you have these people appearing in Srebrenica. And I thought maybe they would not come to Bratunac at all, that Srebrenica was a strategically more interesting municipality and that similar things would happen there as in Bijeljina and Zvornik. However, I was not ruling out the possibility that someone would come to Bratunac as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To summarise, you didn't think it impossible that they would come, but you did not consider it likely or very likely. You didn't expect them to come. Is that a correct understanding of your answer?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's really a nuance, a minor difference. I don't want to make a mistake. I was expecting an event of that kind to take place, but I was not sure that it would indeed happen and in the manner that it eventually did happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the 16th of February, your testimony was: "When I came back to Bratunac, I expected that Bratunac would soon also be caught up in the same problems and that some unit would also appear there."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I never excluded that possibility. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you first find out how many people were killed in the Glogova attack?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never learned the exact number of the people who were killed in Glogova --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Information about the possibility of there having been killings in Glogova, after the funeral of Zekic, someone did mention that people had been murdered in Glogova. However, this person - I cannot remember who it was - was not certain about it. In the course of the several following days, I'm sure I did not have any opportunity to become acquainted with this. I was describing the -- I have described for you the events that took place on the 10th, 11th, and the 12th. Those were very dramatic days. Later, after that period, different information reached me about the events in Glogova. At one point I heard that there had been killings, and then again this would be denied. It is difficult for me to tell you precisely when it was that I learned that killings had taken place. After the war, or rather during the war, I had the opportunity to read a book whose author is a man from Bratunac, and he mentioned in this book that a certain number of people had been killed in Glogova. The author of the book I'm talking about is Mr. Masic, a teacher from Bratunac. After the war, all my attempts to learn more about it were to no avail. It was impossible for me to learn what exactly had happened in Glogova. Some inquiry was done by my lawyers in the course of the preparation of my Defence, and then we learned that, yes, there had been -- that there were killings, and we even discovered the location where it happened. This was all done pursuant to my request because we wanted to establish the truth and find out how many people had been killed in Glogova. However, we were not able to get any firm proof, and I accepted the allegation of the Prosecutor -- the case of the Prosecutor. Whether this is the exact number, I don't know, but I have no reason to doubt what they think happened there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When for the first time you accepted that a large number of people were killed in Glogova? And when I'm talking about a large number of people, that's in the -- over 40, let's say it that way. So I'm not asking about any specific knowledge of whether there was 65 or 68 or 62. When did you accept and believe for the first time that a larger number of people were killed in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, Your Honour, when I was faced with the facts as they were pleaded in the indictment and after we carried out some additional investigation into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Deronjic, let me just see whether I have any more questions for you. Yes, one final question for you. The preparation for the attack on Glogova as far as logistics were concerned, was that prepared prior to the decision taken or was it organised all on the same evening?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was prepared before. The army carried out the preparations. We just gave our approval at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And they were already in position?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. However, the deployment and participation of the units was already known. So right after the meeting, I went to see the unit which had already been lined up in front of the town hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your answers. We'll have a break now because it's already one hour and a half. Would there be any need to ask further questions to Mr. Deronjic on the basis of the questions put by the Bench? Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Not on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understood that we normally would be given an opportunity to ask any questions that arise out of the Prosecution's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if there is some really urgent question. Usually there is after cross-examination, but if it directly arises out of the Prosecution's questions and re-examination, then I would not stop you from putting a question to the witness. But did you have many in mind or...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honour, I didn't. I mean, they're only urgent in the sense that if I don't ask them while Mr. Deronjic is here, then there's not much point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would it take? Should we do it after the break or -- I know that the interpreters and the technicians urgently need a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Probably no more than two or three minutes, Your Honour, if I risk saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're referring to unexpected again. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm just trying to anticipate the remainder of the agenda for today. Does the Court, after Mr. Stewart, -- if we come back and Mr. Stewart asks some additional questions, does the Court intend to ask additional questions? The reason I raise that it because it will take us approximately 25 minutes or 30 minutes to set up for the next witness we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we would have a bit of a longer break - and I'm now looking to the interpreters and the technicians - would you allow for another three minutes, apart from the unexpected?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I get a positive response from the booth. So please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you had a reference to the National Security Council that came up in the questions from Mr. Harmon this afternoon. Did you ever receive any sort of letter or order or written communication of any sort from the National Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Or any oral instruction or order?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So far as the Supreme Command was concerned, you heard a mention from Mr. Harmon as well of Supreme Command. If I suggest to you that that 1 was -- that that was an advisory body, do you know anything at all about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't know anything about the work of such an organ. I'm aware of its existence, but I don't know anything about its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if I suggest to you that Mr. Krajisnik was a member of the Supreme Command from the 31st of December 1992, is that something you can accept, reject, or simply have no knowledge of?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That -- I think that was within the three minutes maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly was. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't want to stimulate a protracted question and answer. But if I could show the witness Prosecution Exhibit 56 to refresh his recollection in respect of one of the questions -- specific questions that was asked by Mr. Stewart, I can elicit a single answer from him. Or I can do it after the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you were asked whether you had ever received any sort of letter or order or written communication of any sort from the National Security Council. And let me direct you to Prosecution Exhibit 56 which you should have in front of you. And I direct your attention to the first paragraph in that order which is dated the 1st of May 1992. Do you see a reference in that first paragraph to the National 1 Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The National Defence -- excuse me, National Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you see that reference?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you see that reference in Prosecution Exhibit 56?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. So, yeah, there has been a mistake. I was not aware of which particular body sent this. When we discussed this decision, I didn't pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Deronjic, this concludes your testimony in this Court. Very often I have to say that I thank witnesses for coming from a long distance. In your case, I think I could just leave it to thanking you for coming and giving evidence in this Court. Mr. Deronjic may be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then just a few technical matters for the parties. I see that no Defence exhibits have been tendered during the cross-examination of Mr. Deronjic, and that the Prosecution tendered Exhibits P33 up to P63. And since no objections were made and since I do not hear any objections at this very moment, they are admitted into evidence. Then finally, I'd like to indicate to the parties, and also to the Registry, that next Monday, and I do understand that the parties have been 1 consulted about it, that next Monday we'll sit in the afternoon and it will be Courtroom III. We'll now adjourn until a quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that the composition of the Prosecution team has changed. Mr. Tieger, could you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'm Alan Tieger. I appear with Mr. Timothy Resch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. We have been provided with four binders as it stands now for the next witness. I do understand that there are a lot more to be expected, and apart from that, that we have binders for footnotes as well which we would not start to learn by heart today. And finally, that there are also a similar number of binders for the original B/C/S version. I do understand that Madam Registrar has a -- has developed a system of numbering these exhibits, and I also do understand that a final number cannot be yet assigned to all the documents because we need the overview of all of it. It's a complex, logistical exercise. Let's start and see where we get stuck, hopefully not at all. Yes. Any questions by the parties as far as the system of numbering is concerned? If not, perhaps, Madam Registrar, a few words on how it works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that each binder will have a number and each binder will contain a certain number of tabs. And since we do not know exactly how many tabs fit into the binder, the final numbering will be done at the end, but the exhibits will be stored in these binders in accordance with their presentation. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I had a bit of difficulty hearing the last portion of the Court's comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said that the exhibits will be stored in these binders in the subsequent order corresponding with their presentation in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And if I may, as long as we're on the subject of logistics in what the Court correctly characterised as a fairly complex logistical exercise, we have also prepared the exhibits in electronic form to be presented in the Sanction mode. In that connection, I should mention that we have been apprised of some of the difficulties that the Court encountered previously. We have made an effort to address and remedy those problems. Whether or not they will be wholly satisfactory, of course, remains to be seen. But I'm optimistic and hopeful that the Sanction presentation will be of greater benefit to the Chamber than it was previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber hopes that it's not necessary to go collectively to the ophthalmologist, I think you call it, because we couldn't just see it. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just say. There are two things actually. I wonder, perhaps I'm just being thick, but I'm just trying to understand. Your Honour says the final numbering will be done at the end. Does Your Honour mean the exhibit numbering or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because it will be double numbering. One for the binder, the next one for the tab. But if we do not know exactly at what number we stop, I mean how many -- I mean, a document could be binder 2, number 14. But if it doesn't fit in, it will be binder 3, number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, it's -- I understand that, Your Honour. That's what I was having difficulty with. I quite see why the binder and tab numbering might have to wait until the end. But they are going to get their P, though, number immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That was what I didn't understand. May I simply make this observation as well: The Defence team in all sorts of ways as Your Honour will know since we -- both counsel are new to this Tribunal, we have been on a learning curve about all sorts of practical matters effecting how the Tribunal works, and Your Honour has been very patient with us as we climb up that learning curve. As far as Sanction is concerned, we are absolutely at the very bottom and beginning of that curve. Because although we know about it, we very assiduously went to a lecture and presentation about it before Christmas. But we have had no training, no experience, we know nothing about it, we know nothing about how it works. I simply make that clear, because if that is going to be a handicap to the Tribunal or to us, then, we'll have to take an opportunity to find out about it. But we know nothing really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what I understand, the Prosecution is presenting it computerwise in Sanction, and we had some difficulties in properly looking at it on our screens. Is Sanction available for the Defence? I take it it is. So therefore -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My understanding, Your Honour, is that it is used by the Defence, for example, in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, except that we are not the Defence in the Brdjanin case. We don't have it. So is it something -- are we going to be given a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the license available? I think, as a matter of fact, Madam Registrar is writing some useful information, as she always does. Let me be wise and wait for it. Yes, if you contact OLAD or Ms. Philpott, the Registrar, then you'll learn more about how available it is, how to use it -- well, whatever information you'd like to have, you can get it from OLAD and the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour. And I hope that money doesn't have to change hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's... I do understand your hope. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to call your next witness, which I do understand will be Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Treanor into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good evening, because it's already after 6.00, Mr. Treanor, I assume. Mr. Treanor, before giving evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Treanor. I noticed that you'd prefer not to have headphones. May I take it that you could follow whatever language is spoken in this Court, that would mean French, English, and/or B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can certainly follow the English, and I can more or less follow the B/C/S. If there's going to be B/C/S, I'll probably use the headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And French?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi usually speaks French, so if he speaks, would you please put on your headphones because otherwise you'll miss what he says. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by reciting quickly some of your academic and professional background, I hope accurately, and I trust you will correct me if I'm in error in any respect. You were -- you received a bachelor of arts in modern languages from the College of Holy Cross in Massachusetts in the United States, a masters degree in Russian and Eastern European studies from Yale University, and a doctor of philosophy from the School of Slavonic and Eastern European Studies from the University of London in Bulgarian history. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if I understand correctly, you began your professional career as an intelligence analyst in the federal research division of the United States Library of Congress in 1977 until 1980. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in 1980, you began work as an historian and later a senior historian at the Department of Justice in the office of special investigations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You remained there until 1994?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, that office is responsible -- was and is responsible for investigating and litigating cases of persons living in or attempting to gain entry to the United States and who are alleged to have participated in Nazi persecution during World War II?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that much of your work in that respect related to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, that is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, from 1994 to the present, have you been engaged first as a research officer for the Office of the Prosecutor, and subsequently as the head of the legal research team, a post you assumed in February of 1998?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I have been a research officer since 1994. There have been some various changes in title. At the beginning, the name of the team that I headed is the leadership research team, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in the course of those efforts, have you conducted your own research and supervised the research efforts of others on your team?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And has that work involved the collection and analysis of documents relating to the conflict in Bosnia, and more specifically, to the Bosnian Serb governmental organs and the SDS?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Treanor, you prepared a report, did you not, entitled "The Bosnian Serb Leadership, 1990 through 1992" which was indicated 30 July 2002?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you -- well, let me ask you quickly whether that report describes the structures, organs of the Serbian Democratic Party and the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, as well as the policies and leadership of the SDS and the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's generally the content of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that report and its accompanying footnotes have been marked as Prosecution's next in order. And at this time, I would ask that it be moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The expert report will be Prosecution Exhibit Number P64. And the 28 binders of footnotes will be P64A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, can you provide the Court with some understanding of the nature of the documents that are reflected in that report and upon which that report relied for its -- for the issues it focussed on and its conclusions.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. First of all, I'd like to say that the report is a joint product written by myself and other members of my unit. I began the research and writing that ultimately resulted in the report in 1994. After the formation of the team in late 1997, early 1998, other members of the team became involved in pursuing the research and writing in specific areas. I continued to supervise that process and maintained ultimate control over what went into the report. Now, the report itself is based on the very extensive collection of original documents which is in the possession of OTP. Most of those documents originate from the Serbian Democratic Party or the governmental structures which it set up, in particular, the Serbian autonomous regions and the various organs of the later Republika Srpska. When I say original documents, I mean documents which were internal to those structures on the one hand, which is a very large volume of documentation including such items as minutes of meetings, internal correspondence, instructions that were issued by various levels, reports received from various levels of the party and state structures. The official documentation also includes the official publication of initially the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina; that is, its Official Gazette, which later became the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska. We also utilise in the report a few press items which helped to shed some light and fill in some gaps in the documentation that we have. There are also -- among the original documentation, there are some diaries of individuals that were involved in the activities of the SDS and its offshoots. And we also drew to some extent on the intercepted telephone conversations of high-ranking members of the SDS. These telephone conversations were intercepted by the State Security Service of Bosnia and Herzegovina and have been made available to us. I think those are the general types of documentation that the report is based on. Primarily, it is based, however, on the -- again, the official documentation of the SDS and its governing structures as they were set up gradually in 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, may I ask -- may I just ask you one clarification. I don't know whether I understood you well. Could you please look at your screen, page 76, line 4. You said: "We also utilise in the report a few press items." I thought I heard something different, but it might be that my ears are not good enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few press items?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, then I misunderstood you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, you've also selected a number of documents for the purposes of assisting the Court in understanding your testimony during the course of this case. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The report is written on a topical basis; that is, each of the structures involved is discussed and analysed from the point of view of how it was organised, how it operated, who the main personalities were, what the nature of its activities were. It is not, as I think it stated in the introduction to the report, the report is not a history by any means of the conflict. Therefore, it does not have a chronological organisation to it, but rather, as I said, a topical organisation. I felt that for the purposes of presenting the report to the Court, it might be more helpful, since I presume the Court is familiar with the report, to attack the subject from another angle, that is, more from the chronological point of view, to give the Court a feeling for the development of events, particularly how the SDS leadership perceived the development of events within Bosnia in order to understand the context in which the various structures that it set up were formed, what their purposes were at the time that they were formed, and how they fulfilled the functions that they were designed to fulfil within the overall plans of the SDS leadership. Therefore, the presentation that you'll be hearing over the next few days will include a number of documents which were not included in the original report in order to give the Court a feeling for this chronological development, the situation as it unfolded for the SDS leaders. We will also be using many documents that were cited in the report, but sometimes, again, attacking those documents from a different angle, more from the point of view of what they tell about the development of events rather than what they tell about the structures per se.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as the Registrar has already noted, the documents to be used during the course of Mr. Treanor's testimony have been assembled and presented. At this time, I would ask that they be given the next order in number and moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit Number P65.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, as we move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you would expect a decision on admission into evidence, Mr. Tieger, but the practice in this Trial Chamber is that we deal finally with the exhibits at the very end of the testimony of the witness. But of course, the Defence knows that they could object right away. But in order not to do it all in bits and pieces, we do it at the very end, but we'll hear whatever objection there might be at the moment when the documents are tendered. And that of course -- and since we're talking now about binders, the Defence is in a position to object whatever document from a binder is presented, and if they would find there would be any reason not to be admitted, not even to be presented to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I'd like to move into that chronology, but perhaps before we do, it would be of assistance to the Chamber if you could provide an overview of the materials that you will cover, the issues that you will address during the course of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The report, as I mentioned earlier, is organised on a topical basis. The main topics covered are the Serbian Democratic Party itself, its founding, its programme, development and activities, the policies that its leadership pursued. It then moves into discussing the structures that were set up by the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party; that is, the -- first of all, the regional structures, and then the central governmental organs of what later became Republika Srpska. The presentation over the next few days will cover all of those topics. But as I indicated earlier, we'll attempt to put them into the context of the development of events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which I will try to refer to as BH for the sake of simplicity heretofore, between approximately the middle of 1990 and the end of 1992. That period of time saw Bosnia and Herzegovina move from being under the single-party rule of the League of Communists to being a -- to having a short-lived perhaps multiparty governance, and then finally moving into what the Bosnian Serb Assembly later referred to as an interethnic and interfaith war. The main milestones along that path are the -- and as will be covered in the presentation, the founding of the political parties, especially the SDS, in July 1990, the multiparty elections in November and December 1990, then the developments of relations between the SDS, which became one of the governing parties in BH after the elections, and its partners in governance in a coalition. They were in a coalition with the SDA, the party of democratic action, which was a Bosnian Muslim party, and the Croatian Democratic Union, which was the Croatian party in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Their relations began to deteriorate over certain issues, most notably the position of Bosnia and Herzegovina within Yugoslavia, the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina itself. Those relations were exacerbated by the outbreak of war hostilities in Slovenia and Croatia in the summer of 1991, which led to a heightening of tensions within Bosnia, which produced the next major step in the development of this story which is October 1991 when the Assembly of BH basically voted to take BH on the path to total independence from Yugoslavia, which was responded to by the SDS leadership with the formation of its own assembly in October 1991. That further develops -- they further developed their governmental institutions over the next few months. Negotiations were going on at the same time to reach an internal settlement. But they failed. And at the beginning of April 1992, BH was, in fact, recognised by foreign powers as an independent state which led the SDS leadership, and in particular, the Assembly which it had founded, to declare RS as an independent state. The story then continues, as will be seen in the course of the presentation, with the activities of the higher level government bodies of Republika Srpska, in particular the National Security Council and the Presidency of Republika Srpska which -- of which Mr. Krajisnik was a member. And we take the story through, I think, until the -- basically the middle of December 1991 [sic] when the Presidency of Republika Srpska was reformed, and Radovan Karadzic was elected as the single president of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you just -- I think --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a minor correction to the record. I think when you concluded, you mentioned that the -- we take the story I think until the -- basically the middle of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: 1992, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Treanor, will the documents to which you refer and your discussion of those documents also embrace the leadership figures of the SDS and Republika Srpska and the nature of their interaction with each other and their subordinates?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's fair to say that the documentation that will be presented focuses very much on the central leadership figures within the SDS and its governmental structures and the relationships that they had with each other and also with many of their subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, then, can we begin discussing the documents that you selected, and perhaps we can begin, then, with the founding assembly of the SDS in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Your Honours, this can be found at tab 1 of binder 1 and will, of course, be presented on your screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, can you tell us what the document found at tab 1 represents.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, if I'm not mistaken, we have here the introductory speech of Radovan Karadzic to the founding assembly of the Serbian Democratic Party on the 19th of July 1990. It was -- this Assembly founded the party, elected Radovan Karadzic president of the party, and adopted a programme and party statutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Although I know you've already alluded to it in your overview, can you place the foundation of the Serbian Democratic Party in context of events in former Yugoslavia and in Bosnia particularly.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I'm not sure how great a length you'd like me to go on about that, seeing as there's only a few minutes left. To make a very long story short, Yugoslavia was going through a very severe crisis in 1989 and 1990. There was acute disagreement among the ruling communist elites in the various republics who still ruled Yugoslavia as a one-party state. Disagreement over the internal structure of that state, the nature of its political system, and indeed its economic system. I would also remind the Court that at this time the communist systems in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union were also undergoing severe crisis, the fall of the Berlin Wall on the 9th of November 1989, and I could recall a little closer to Yugoslavia the fall of the Ceausescu regime and the murder of Ceausescu on the 25th of December 1989. The League of Communists of Yugoslavia had an extraordinary -- its 14th and extraordinary congress on -- in January 1990, and on the 23rd of January, that congress, in fact, broke up to disagreements among the representatives, delegates to that congress, from the various republics. That effectively ended one-party rule in Yugoslavia and opened the way for multiparty elections in the various republics. 1990 just happened to be an election year in Yugoslavia, the previous elections having been four years earlier. And one of the issues during the decade prior to that within Yugoslavia had been the issue of the nature of the political system and whether it should be transformed into a multiparty system. The pressure for that was now -- proved to be irresistible. Multiparty elections were scheduled in the various republics. They took -- multiparty elections took place in Slovenia first, on the 8th of April 1990, followed by Croatia on the 22nd of April. Both sets of elections resulted in severe defeats for the communist -- leagues of communists in those republics and brought to power nationalistic parties in both of those republics who were by no means committed to the continued existence of Yugoslavia. Now, in Bosnia, in February 1990, a law had been passed which permitted the founding of noncommunist political parties. However, there was a clause in that law which forbade any political associations founded on an ethnic or religious basis, which proved to be controversial. That clause was overturned by the constitutional court on the 11th of June 1990. And at the end of July 1990, the 31st of July, a package of constitutional amendments to the constitution of BH came into force which, in effect, abolished the monopoly of the League of Communists, dismantled the communists' ideological provisions of the constitution, guaranteed the right of free political association, and it also had a couple of other interesting clauses which became the subject of some controversy later on, so I will allude to them. Amendment 60 defined Bosnia-Herzegovina as a democratic sovereign state of its citizens and peoples and named the Muslim, Serbian, and Croatian peoples. It also, in Amendment 62, specified that the territory of BH was indivisible, and the boundaries of the republic could only be changed at a referendum of the citizens with a two-thirds majority. At any rate, the way was open for the founding of noncommunist political parties and for the holding of multiparty elections. In fact, on the 6th of August, elections were scheduled for the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, I don't know whether this is a suitable moment to stop you. But I look at the clock, it's 7.00 o'clock. We have to finish. And you showed already -- a limited time, but if you have one or two more sentences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but certainly not more, because it's not just us, it's also the interpreters and the technicians who assist us. Please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The foundation of the noncommunist political parties had already begun. On the 26th of May 1990, the SDA, the party of democratic action, was formed. That was before the constitutional court rulings, so its name does not carry an ethnic appellation, but it was certainly based on the concerns of the Muslim people, and it was -- it came out for -- in its programme for the maintenance of BH within its present borders. I'll just mention the HDZ before we get on to the SDS, where we can pick up tomorrow. The HDZ was founded on the 18th of August in 1990 as the Croatian National Party in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And on the primary issue of the day, that is, the future of BH, its position was that BH should be enabled to exercise the right of self-determination up to and including secession from Yugoslavia. So that is the context in which the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party. Was founded in July 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Treanor. We'll adjourn. We'll continue tomorrow in the afternoon, quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom. I instruct you not to speak with anyone, not even someone in the office of your employer, about your testimony that you have given in this Court and you're still about to give in this Court. If there's nothing else to be raised by the parties, we'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 20th day of February, 2004, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
